title: Shopping
goal: Shop for groceries: name quantities, ask about prices, and point to the item you mean.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — An der Käsetheke
dialogs.intro: Saturday morning, and the supermarket is packed. Budi is shopping for the week and stops at the cheese counter — the only spot in a German supermarket still served by a human.

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Der Nächste, bitte! Was darf es sein?
lines.id: Next, please! What can I get you?
lines.literal: the next, please! what may it be?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich hätte gern zweihundert Gramm Käse.
lines.id: I'd like two hundred grams of cheese.
lines.literal: I would-have gladly two-hundred gram cheese.

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Welchen Käse möchten Sie? Wir haben Gouda, Emmentaler und Bergkäse.
lines.id: Which cheese would you like? We have Gouda, Emmentaler and Bergkäse.
lines.literal: which cheese would-like you? we have Gouda, Emmentaler and mountain-cheese.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Diesen hier, bitte. Wie viel kostet er?
lines.id: This one here, please. How much is it?
lines.literal: this-one here, please. how much costs he?

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Zwei Euro neunzig pro hundert Gramm. Sonst noch etwas?
lines.id: Two euros ninety per hundred grams. Anything else?
lines.literal: two euro ninety per hundred gram. otherwise still something?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, ein Kilo Tomaten und drei Bananen.
lines.id: Yes, a kilo of tomatoes and three bananas.
lines.literal: yes, one kilo tomatoes and three bananas.

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Obst und Gemüse müssen Sie selbst wiegen. Dort hinten.
lines.id: You have to weigh fruit and vegetables yourself. Over there at the back.
lines.literal: fruit and vegetables must you yourself weigh. there at-the-back.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ach so. Und haben Sie noch Milch?
lines.id: Oh, I see. And do you still have milk?
lines.literal: ah so. and have you still milk?

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Ja, hinten links. Eine Flasche oder eine Packung?
lines.id: Yes, at the back on the left. Bottle or carton?
lines.literal: yes, at-the-back left. a bottle or a pack?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zwei Packungen, bitte. Das ist alles.
lines.literal: two packs, please. that is all.

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Gut. Dann macht das zusammen vierzehn Euro zwanzig.
lines.id: Fine. Then that comes to fourteen euros twenty.
lines.literal: good. then makes that together fourteen euro twenty.

lines.speaker: Verkäuferin:
lines.text: Die kostet extra. Die meisten Leute bringen eine Tasche mit.
lines.id: Bags cost extra. Most people bring their own shopping bag.
lines.literal: that costs extra. the most people bring a carry-bag.

notes: ***Ich hätte gern…*** is the politest way to ask for something, and in shops it has nearly replaced *Ich möchte*. It's a conditional form, but just use it as a set phrase — the grammar comes apart in A2.

***Was darf es sein?*** literally "what may it be?", meaning "what can I get you?". It's the standard line at every bread, meat and cheese counter in Germany. All you need to answer is: *Ich hätte gern…*

**Units don't take a plural after a number.** *zwei **Kilo***, *drei **Stück***, *fünf **Euro***, *hundert **Gramm*** — no plural ending. What **does** go plural is the container: *zwei **Packungen***, *drei **Flaschen***. This seemingly tiny rule is clearly audible to German ears.

**Line 4: *Diesen hier*.** *Dieser* ("this") behaves exactly like *der*, including turning into *diesen* in the Akkusativ. Pointing at an item and saying *Diesen hier, bitte* is the safest way to shop while your vocabulary is still small.

**Line 4 also uses *er* for the cheese.** Because *der Käse* is masculine, the pronoun is *er*, not *es*. Where English says "it" for every object, German calls things *er* or *sie* according to their article — and it sounds perfectly natural once you're used to it.
***Obst und Gemüse*** almost always come as a pair, and both are **uncountable**: there's no *zwei Obst*. You buy *ein Kilo Obst* or name the kind: *drei Äpfel*, *zwei Bananen*.

grammars.title: Quantities and containers
body: Grocery shopping is almost entirely number + unit + item, with no word in between: *ein Kilo Tomaten*, *eine Flasche Wasser*, *zweihundert Gramm Käse* — where English says "a kilo **of** tomatoes", German just leaves the "of" out.
after: ⚠️ In Germany *ein Pfund* means **500 grams**, not an English pound (454 grams). At markets and meat counters it's still used every day, even though it was officially replaced by the kilogram long ago.

Asking about prices comes in two forms you need to keep apart: ***Wie viel kostet** das?* for one item, and ***Wie viel kosten** die Tomaten?* for plural items. What changes is the verb, which follows the item — just like English "how much **is** it" vs. "how much **are** they".

grammars.title: welcher and dieser — choosing and pointing
body: These two words behave exactly like *der/die/das*: their ending follows the gender and changes in the Akkusativ. If you already know *der → den*, you already know *dieser → diesen*.
after: Notice that the endings match the last letter of *der*, *die*, *das* exactly: **-er**, **-e**, **-es**. Once you see that pattern, the whole table above stops feeling like something new to memorize.

In everyday conversation people usually shorten it: *Welchen?* ("which one?") and *Diesen hier* ("this one") without repeating the noun at all. Those two words, plus your index finger, are enough to buy anything.

blocks.text: At the checkout you'll also often hear ***Haben Sie es passend?*** — "do you have the exact change?". Answering *Nein, tut mir leid* is perfectly fine; the question is only about giving change.
The name of a shop also tells you what it sells, and almost all of them are built the same way: product + *-ei*, or + *Laden/Geschäft*.

blocks.title: Three things that surprise newcomers
items: **Bottles carry a deposit (*Pfand*).** You pay 8–25 cents extra per bottle and get it back when you return it to the machine at the supermarket. Don't throw your bottles away — they're money.
**German cashiers are very fast.** Items fly down the belt and you're expected to bag them at the same speed. Many people pack first and pay afterwards.
**Sunday really is closed.** Except for some bakeries, train stations and the Späti. Doing your weekly shopping on Saturday isn't a tip, it's a plan.
